activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The rhyme 'One, Two, Buckle My Shoe' puts the counting words into a rhyme.
story:
Paisley stood at the toy shelf at daycare. She wanted all ten blocks for her tower. Ten blocks made a tall, tall tower.

She picked up one block. Then two blocks. Then she stopped. What came after two? She looked at her hands. She squeezed her eyes. The next number hid from her, like a cat under a bed.

Her friend Milo sat close by. "Sing it," said Milo. "Sing the shoe song." Paisley knew the shoe song. It went with a clap. She clapped and sang, "One, two, buckle my shoe." The words felt like a joke that tickled her ears. One rhymed with two in the song, and the song pulled the next number out.

"Three!" said Paisley. She put down block three. She sang the song again with Milo. "Three, four, shut the door." Four blocks sat in a line. The song kept giving her numbers, five and six, then seven and eight, then nine and ten.

The tower stood tall and wobbly. It smelled like soap and wood. Milo clapped a loud clap. The tower tipped over and fell with a big crash. Paisley laughed and rubbed her toes, because one block had landed on her shoe.

"Again," said Milo. Paisley picked up one block, then two, and sang the shoe song again, all the way to ten.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: You can often tell how a friend feels by looking at their face.
story:
Julia held her teddy bear, Ben. Bedtime was here. But Ben looked sad. His mouth was turned down. Julia knew that face. Mama made that face when she lost her keys.

"Are you sad, Ben?" she asked.

She looked under the bed. She found one red sock. She stuck the sock on Ben's paw like a mitten. Ben still looked sad. Julia made a frown too. Then she made a big smile. Ben did not smile back. Teddies cannot move their mouths.

Then Julia saw it. Ben's other paw was empty. His little blue shirt was gone! It had fallen behind the pillow.

Julia pulled it out. She dressed Ben in his shirt. She hugged him close. He smelled sweet, like soap and sleep.

"Now you are happy," Julia said. She tucked him in. His soft head rested by her cheek.

"Night night, sweet Ben," said Mama from the door.

Julia closed her eyes and whispered, "Big smile in the morning."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Chocolate can make dogs very sick, so dogs are never given chocolate.
story:
Jack walked home with Dad. He held the little dog's leash. The dog was small and brown. His name was Bingo.

Bingo wagged his tail on the sunny street. Jack had a chocolate coin in his pocket. He wanted to give it to Bingo. "Treat for you!" said Jack.

Dad shook his head. "Not that one," he said. "Chocolate can make dogs very sick. Dogs are never given chocolate." Dad held out a shiny bag. Inside was a bone-shaped dog treat. "Offer this instead," said Dad.

Jack held the treat on his flat hand, like a spoon full of cereal. Bingo took it gently. Then Bingo licked Jack's fingers. Jack laughed and began to sing a happy song. Birds sang too, from the big green tree.

At home, Dad poured water into a shiny bowl. Bingo drank it all up. Jack patted his soft head. "Good dog," said Jack. "I will keep you safe."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use.
story:
Jacob ran into the backyard with his grandpa. The grass was green and soft. Jacob wanted to find a brown bug.

He looked under a big leaf. He looked by the old red pot. Then he saw something small on the ground. It was shiny and black. It was a little lighter.

Jacob wanted to pick it up. His hand went out. But then he stopped. He remembered something. Matches and lighters were only for grown-ups.

"Grandpa!" Jacob called. "Come and see!" Grandpa came right away. He looked at the little black lighter.

"Thank you, Jacob," said Grandpa. "You did not touch it. That was safe and smart." Grandpa picked up the lighter. He put it high in his pocket.

Grandpa sat down on the step. Jacob sat next to him, close and safe. Grandpa shared his big sun hat with Jacob. They sat and looked for bugs together.

A little brown bug crawled up the step. "There he is!" said Jacob. Grandpa smiled and held Jacob's hand.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: We ask before we take something that belongs to someone else.
story:
Charles sat at the dinner table. He saw a big plate with blue flowers. Mom had painted the flowers long ago. The plate was Sam's special plate today.

Charles wanted it. He reached out fast. He took the plate right off Sam's mat. "Hey!" said Sam. His face went red. He put his head down on his arms.

Charles looked at Sam. Then he looked at the plate. He pushed it back across the table. "Sam, may I have the flower plate?" he asked. Sam sat up. He smiled a little. "You can have it after me," said Sam. "Then we can take turns." Dad gave Charles a plain white plate. It clinked when it touched the table. The warm bread smelled sweet.

Charles ate his bread. The plate went back and forth, back and forth, back and forth. Sam laughed. Charles laughed too. Baby Ivy fell asleep in her chair. "Can we use the flower plate tomorrow?" Charles asked. "Yes," said Sam. "You can ask me again then." Charles took one more bite and slid the plate over to Sam.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A season is all the practices and games a team plays from start to end.
story:
Brooks was on the swim team. He had a towel with sheep on it. He hid his goggles in the towel after every practice.

At the pool, the water was cool and blue. It smelled like chlorine. Brooks kicked his legs and splashed. His coach said, "Big arms, Brooks!"

One day Brooks asked his dad, "How long is the team?" Dad held up the schedule. It had lines and numbers. Dad pointed to the top. "This was our first practice." He pointed to the bottom. "This is our last game." Dad let Brooks count the games left. Brooks touched each line. "One, two, three games left!"

So the team was all of it. Every practice. Every game. From the first line to the last line.

Brooks swam at the last game. The water went swish, swish. He touched the wall and looked up. Dad waved the sheep towel high in the air. "Last one, Brooks!" Dad called. "Then we get ice cream."

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: In Japan, people say 'itadakimasu' before eating to give thanks for the food.
story:
Aiden put on his boot. He pulled and pulled. Then Grandma laughed. "One boot is enough inside," she said. "We need to go to the big hall now."

At the hall there were tables and bowls of rice. Aiden wanted to eat fast. Grandma held his hands. "First we say itadakimasu," she said. "People in Japan say it before eating. It gives thanks for the food."

Aiden tried. "Ita... dakki... moose!" Everyone giggled. "Was that true? Did I say it?" he asked.

"Not quite," said Grandma. "Try again, slow."

"Ita-da-ki-ma-su," said Aiden.

"That's it!" Grandma clapped.

Then the bowls went click, click, click. Everyone picked up chopsticks together. Aiden ate his rice. "Grandma, do we say it again for more rice?"

"No, silly boy. Once is just right."

Aiden grinned and held out his bowl. "More, please!"

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Glasses help some people see more clearly.
story:
Kayden wants a story. He runs to Grandpa with his book. "Read to me, please!"

Grandpa pats the chair. Kayden sits close. He hears Grandpa's chair go squeak, squeak. His ears hear that. His nose smells warm soup in the pot. Mom made soup for the cold winter day.

But Grandpa does not open the book. Grandpa looks and looks. "Where are my glasses?" he says. Kayden touches the soft cushion with his hands. No glasses there. He looks under the blanket with his eyes. There they are! He gives them to Grandpa.

Grandpa puts them on. Now he opens the book. He reads the whole story, nice and clear. Kayden licks his lips. He tastes sweet apple after the story. "Grandpa, do the glasses help you?" asks Kayden. Grandpa smiles. "Yes, they help me see the words." Kayden hugs him and counts, "One story, one apple, one happy Grandpa!"

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: In and out are opposites.
story:
Blake was at daycare. She wanted to build a big tower. She put the blocks in a box one by one. Then baby Sam came over. Sam pulled the blocks out of the box. "Hey!" said Blake. "My blocks!" Sam laughed and clapped.

Miss Jo came to talk with them. "Sam is small," she said. "You are big. He wants to play too." Blake watched Sam drop a block out of the box. Then Blake put one in. Sam took it out. In went a block. Out it came. It was like a fast game, then a slow game.

Blake had an idea. She gave Sam one box alone. Sam put blocks in. He took them out. He was happy. Blake built her tower next to him. It grew tall. Sam patted the top block. "Yay!" said Blake. "We did it, Sam."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: The author is the person who wrote the words of a book.
story:
Theodore went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about a spider. "Find the picture," said the librarian, Miss Amy. Theodore looked and looked. He found a book with a spider on the front. He opened it in the middle. "That is not the start," said Miss Amy. "Turn back to the front." Theodore turned the pages, one, two, three. The first page said: The words go from front to back.

"Who made up this spider?" Theodore asked. Miss Amy pointed to the cover. "The author wrote the words," she said. "See the name? That is the author." Theodore read the name out loud. Then he turned page after page, one, two, three, all the way to the end.

The spider in the story fell asleep. Theodore leaned on his mom. "I like the author," he said. "Can we bake cookies at home?"

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Two people can feel differently about the same thing.
story:
Clara ran to the music corner at school. A big purple drum sat there, just her size. She hit it once. Boom! Clara laughed. She hit it again and again. Boom, boom, boom!

Ben put his hands over his ears. He ran to the rug and sat far away. Clara stopped. She felt confused. She loved the drum, but Ben did not.

She walked over to Ben. "Too loud," he said. Clara looked at her drum. Then she looked at Ben. Maybe they could like different things.

"Come with me," she said. Ben followed her to the toy shelf. Clara found the magnet toys. Click! One magnet jumped onto another. Ben smiled a big smile. Clara was excited. "You try," she said.

Ben stuck two magnets together. Click! Now the quiet sounds filled the corner. Clara clapped. Ben filled a long chain, all purple and blue.

Then the chain stuck to the chair leg. Neither of them could pull it off. Ben laughed so hard he fell over. Clara laughed too.

The teacher came by. "You two look happy," she said. Clara nodded. "Ben likes quiet. I like loud," she said. She held up the magnet chain. "We both like this!"

"Want to drum soft?" asked Ben. Clara tapped the drum very slowly. Pum, pum. Ben tapped too. "I like that," he said.

Clara grinned. Two friends, one drum, both smiling.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: On the school bus, children stay sitting in their seats.
story:
Sofia stood in the school hallway with her mama. It was her first day of school. The hallway smelled like new crayons. Sofia held a red backpack on her back.

A big yellow bus stopped outside the window. Sofia pressed her nose to the glass. Could she see the children? Yes! They sat in little seats, two by two. One boy stood up. He wanted to wave out the window. Then the driver spoke to him. What did she say? The boy sat back down in his seat. His hand came out the window and waved from where he sat.

"Look, Mama," said Sofia. "He waves and he sits." The bus door opened with a whoosh. The children came out one by one. The waving boy ran past Sofia in the hallway. He had a red jacket, red like her backpack.

"Were the seats comfy?" Sofia asked him. The boy nodded. "You get to sit the whole way," he said. Sofia smiled. Maybe she would ride the bus one day too. She gave her mama a hug and walked to her classroom door.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: A cup with nothing in it is empty, and a cup filled to the top is full.
story:
John sat in his big car seat. The car went fast, then slow. "Stop," said Mom. The car stopped at the snack shop.

John was hungry. Mom bought him a cold drink and a warm muffin. The sun was hot outside. The drink was cold in his hands.

Mom filled a little cup with water for John. She poured it slow. The cup got full, all the way to the top. Then Mom showed John the other cup. It had nothing in it. It was empty. John looked at the full cup. He looked at the empty cup. He took a little sip. Now the full cup was not so full.

Back in the car, John saw a big dog and a small dog outside the window. Mom had a bone in a bag for the big dog at home. "We will give him this," she said. John held his cup with two hands. He took small sips, one by one.

The cup was light now. Soon it was empty. Mom wiped his mouth with a clean, soft cloth. The car went fast again. John waved his empty cup at the small dog going by.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Covering different holes on a recorder makes different notes.
story:
Maya ran into the garage. She found a little flute in Daddy's old bag. It was white and had holes on top. "I will play a song!" she said.

Maya blew into it. Squeak! The sound was not a song. It was a squeak. Maya tried again. Squeak! "My flute is silly," she said. Then she looked at her fingers. One finger was not on a hole all the way. She put it down flat. She blew once more. Toot! A real note came out! Maya jumped up and down.

She lifted one finger. Toot, a new note! She put the finger back. The old note came back. She lifted a different finger. Another new note! "Listen, Daddy!" she called. Daddy ran in fast. Maya played toot, toot, toot. She said, "This one is my song. It goes toot and toot and toot!"

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A coach teaches the team and helps the players learn the game.
story:
Zayn put on his red shirt. It was team day at the community center. One, two, three, four, five kids ran onto the floor. The coach blew her whistle.

Zayn did not know where to stand. He stood by the door. The ball flew past him. "Zayn, come here," the coach called. She pointed to a spot on the floor. "Stand right here." Zayn stood on the spot. The ball came again. This time he caught it. He threw it to his friend Mia. She waved her arms high.

How did that happen? Zayn looked at the coach. She showed Ben where to stand too. Then she showed Sam. Then the whole team knew.

After the game, they drank cold water. One, two, three, four, five cups. Zayn fell down on the mat, laughing. "Same spot next week?" asked the coach. "Yes!" said Zayn.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Teammates can cheer for each other, even when someone misses.
story:
William put on his small swim vest. It was morning at the pool. His swim team was ready to play a ball game in the shallow water.

The coach blew her whistle. "Pass the ball to your friends!" she said. William kicked his legs and stayed close to his teammate Mia. The water was cool and splashed his chin.

Mia threw the ball to William. He reached out his hands. The ball hit his fingers and went plop into the water. It bobbed away. William's face went hot. He wanted to hide.

But then his team began to shout. "Try again, William!" said Mia. "You can do it!" said Ben. Even the coach clapped her hands. William grabbed the ball from the water. He took a big breath. He threw it back to Mia.

Mia caught it! Everyone cheered again. William laughed and splashed his feet. Now it was Ben's turn. Ben missed the ball too. The ball went over his head and splashed the coach.

"Try again, Ben!" William called out loud. He clapped his wet hands. Ben picked up the ball and smiled. The game went on until the morning sun was high. "One more throw," said Mia, holding up the ball.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: A library card lets you borrow books and take them home to read.
story:
Lily ran to the reading corner. A big red book sat on the shelf. The cover felt rough, like a cat's tongue. She opened it. A dragon filled the page. The dragon blew fire at a castle. "Wow," said Lily. "Big fire!"

Lily wanted this book. She hugged it to her chest. She walked to the desk. "I want to keep it," she said. The librarian smiled. "You can take it home," she said. "You just need a card." Lily patted her pockets. "I don't have a card," she said. Her tummy felt wobbly. The librarian laughed. "Today you get your very first one!"

Lily said her name. The librarian typed it. Then she handed Lily a small blue card. Lily held it up high. "My card!" she said. "Look what it does!" The librarian put the book in a bag. "The card lets you take books home," she said. Lily clapped. "Then the dragon can come to my house!"

That night, Lily's coat hung on its hook. The rough red book sat on her bed. Daddy read one page. The dragon blew fire again. Lily giggled and pulled the blanket up to her chin. "He can't get me," she whispered. "He is just paper." Then she patted the dragon's nose and said, "Good night, dragon. Back to the library tomorrow."

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Saying 'excuse me' is a polite way to get past someone who is in your way.
story:
Ethan was a knight at school. His cape was a red towel. He had to save the teddy bear from the block tower. But the way was blocked. Maya and Sam stood in the door, building a long train.

Ethan tried to squeeze past. He bumped the train. A car fell off. "Oh no," said Ethan. "Sorry, Sam." Sam picked up the car. He put it back on the train. Ethan stepped back. Now what?

Then he remembered the magic words. "Excuse me," said Ethan, in his best gentle knight voice. Maya smiled. She moved her feet to the side. Sam moved too. The way was clear! Ethan walked past, slow and careful, like a cat.

"Thank you!" said Ethan. He ran to the tower. He lifted the teddy bear up high. "The bear is safe!" The class clapped. Ethan bowed in his red cape. "Excuse me," said a small voice behind him. It was Maya, holding two cookies. "Do you want one?" Ethan grinned. "Yes, please!"

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your fingertips can tell if something is soft, rough, smooth or bumpy.
story:
Colton ran to the guessing table at daycare. Miss Ana had a big smile. "Close your eyes," she said. "Feel and guess!"

Colton shut his eyes tight. He could not see a thing. But his ears heard his friends giggling. His nose smelled the orange slices for snack time.

Miss Ana put something in his hands. Colton touched it with his fingertips. It felt bumpy all over. "A pinecone!" he shouted. He opened his eyes. Yes! It was a pinecone!

Next came something soft and light. His fingertips said soft like a baby chick. "A feather!" It was a feather. Last came something cool and smooth, like a stone from the creek. "A rock!" Colton laughed.

"You can feel with your fingers!" said his friend Mia. Colton nodded big. At snack time he licked his orange slice. Yummy and sour! Then he touched his messy, sticky hands and giggled all the way to the sink.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: You can show how old you are by holding up that many fingers.
story:
Today was Ellie's birthday party in her classroom. Her mom helped her hang paper stars on the wall. Her dad brought a big cake. Friends came in with balloons. Even the class owl puppet sat on the shelf, watching.

A new boy named Sam ran up to Ellie. "How old are you?" he asked. Ellie held up her fingers. She looked at her hand. "One, two, three," she counted. Three fingers stood up. "No, wait," she said. She wiggled her little finger up too. "One, two, three, four!" Sam laughed and held up four fingers too. "We are the same!" he said.

Then all the friends held up four fingers. "Happy birthday, Ellie!" they shouted. Ellie blew out the candles with her dad's help. She was not three anymore, and her fingers showed it. "Four fingers for four years," she said, and she wiggled them at the owl puppet too.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When you feel excited, you might want to jump, bounce or shout.
story:
Lucy went to the park with her dad. Grandma was coming to meet them there. Lucy could not wait. She felt so excited. She jumped up and down. She bounced on her toes. She shouted, "Grandma! Grandma!" But Grandma was not there yet.

Lucy looked down the path. She looked with one eye, then two eyes. No Grandma. Lucy felt sad. Her jumps got smaller and smaller. Then a big dog ran near, and Lucy felt scared. Dad held her hand. The dog's owner called it back. Lucy felt angry at the dog for a minute. Then it licked her shoe, and she laughed.

"You are bouncing a lot," said Dad. "Let's wait in a calm way." They sat on the bench. Lucy colored with her chalk on the ground. She drew a big red heart for Grandma. She waited. She waited some more. Waiting felt long, but her chalk kept her hands busy.

Then a voice said, "Is that heart for me?" It was Grandma! Lucy jumped up one more time, because now jumping was just right. Grandma picked her up and hugged her tight. "I saw your red heart all the way down the path," said Grandma. Lucy smiled a big smile.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: At a concert, people in the audience clap when the music is over to show they enjoyed it.
story:
Everly sat in a big red seat. Her mama sat next to her. On the stage, a woman began to play a quiet song on a violin. Everly liked it a lot. She wanted to clap right away. So she clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap.

A man in front turned around. He put one finger near his lips. Everly stopped clapping. She looked at mama. "Wait," mama whispered. "Watch the song. It is not over yet." So Everly waited. The music went up and down. It went soft and slow. Then it stopped. The stage got very still. Now the man in front began to clap. Then everyone clapped at once. Everly clapped too. It was like a game. The song ends, and then the hands go.

Next came a fast song. Everly wanted to play this game too. She listened hard. The song had a steady beat. She tried to clap along with it. She clapped too fast. She tried again. Too slow. She kept trying. Then her claps landed right on the beat. Clap, clap, clap, clap. She was with the song. Mama clapped along too.

At the end, the woman on stage sang a song Everly knew. It was about a star. Everly sang the words from memory. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Her voice was small but strong. The song ended. Everly held her hands up high. She waited and waited. Then the whole hall clapped, loud and long. Everly clapped the biggest clap of all. "Again," she said. "Sing it again."

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: A pencil needs sharpening when its tip gets dull, and a grown-up can help.
story:
Nathan sat at the big writing club table. He had a wide piece of paper and a pencil. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

He gripped the pencil in his fist. He made a line for the letter N. But the line was fat and fuzzy. "Why is my line so big?" he asked. Miss Amy leaned close. "Let's look at your pencil," she said. The tip was dull and flat.

Miss Amy took the pencil to the sharpener. She turned it around and around. Then she gave it back. The tip was small and pointy now. Nathan made his line again. This time it was thin and neat.

He wrote N, then A, then T. "I did it!" he said. Miss Amy put a little hat sticker on his paper. Nathan smiled so wide. "Can I write it again?" he asked. "Yes," said Miss Amy. "Write it one more time." And he did.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer and basketball, the referee blows a whistle to stop play.
story:
Margot sat on the big red cushion. The soccer game was on TV. Everyone was there. Dad was there. Grandma was there. Even her cousin Ben was there. Dad carried a plate of warm popcorn. He set it down on the low table. "Careful, it is warm," he said. Margot took one small piece and blew on it.

The players ran and ran. They kicked the ball. Then Margot heard a loud sound. Tweet, tweet! She covered her ears. "Why did everyone stop running?" she asked. "The man in the black shirt blew his whistle," said Grandma. "Watch." Margot watched. The whistle blew again. Tweet, tweet! The players stopped. They stood still like statues.

Margot wanted to try. She held her toy whistle. Tweet, tweet! she blew. Ben laughed. Nobody stood still. Dad kept munching popcorn. Grandma kept waving her sock in the air like a lazy flag. Margot laughed too. "My whistle does not stop Dad," she said. She blew it again. Tweet, tweet! Ben jumped up and hurried to the kitchen for juice. "Look!" said Margot. "It stopped Ben!"

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Seeds need water to start growing.
story:
Jordan planted seeds in the school garden. He made a deep little hole for each one. Then he patted the soft dirt on top.

Every day Jordan ran to the garden. He looked for his seeds. Nothing came up. The dirt was dry and hard. Next to him, Mia had little green leaves. She held a watering can.

Jordan wanted green leaves too. He found his own small watering can. He gave his seeds a gentle drink of water. He sat in a circle with his friends to wait.

The next day, Jordan ran to the garden again. Something tiny and green was peeking out of the dirt. Jordan clapped his hands. "Hello, little plant," he said. He filled the watering can again. "Would you like to share my water?"

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: A book in English starts at the front cover, and you turn the pages until you reach the back.
story: Ethan wanted his bedtime story. He ran to get his book about a dog. Dad was still typing on his computer. So Ethan tried to read it himself. He opened the book. But he opened it from the back. The pages looked all mixed up. The dog was wet. Then the dog was in his bed. Then the dog began to bark at nothing. Ethan turned a page. The dog was lost. Ethan turned another page. The dog was home. "That is not right," said Ethan. Dad came over. He sat on the edge of the bed. Ethan held up the book. "It is all jumbled," he said. Dad tapped the front of the book. Ethan looked. The front had the dog's happy face on it. Ethan flipped the book over. He opened the front cover. There was page one. The dog woke up in the morning. Ethan turned the pages one by one. The story went along, calm and long, all the way to the back. The last page said good night to the dog. Ethan yawned. He handed the book to Dad. "Read it again," he said, "from the front."

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes.
story:
William jumped into the car with a big bag. "Time for Grandma's house!" said Mom. The bag held gifts for Grandma's new puppy. William could not wait.

The bag tipped over on the seat. Everything fell out! William reached for the toys. A ball rolled under his feet. A squeaky duck sat on his lap. Then he found a bouncy sock. William laughed. "Socks don't go with toys!" He waved the sock in the air.

"Silly me," said Mom. "That sock fell in from the laundry. Socks go with clothes, like shirts and hats." William put the sock in a little pile with a hat and a shirt. Then he made a toy pile. Then a food pile, with crackers and a banana.

"Grandma will love her snacks," said Mom. "And the puppy will love that duck." William hugged the duck. It let out a big squeak. "Beep beep!" said William. "Almost there," said Mom, and pointed out the window at Grandma's red door.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange.
story:
Michael was at Grandma's house. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. Grandma put the pumpkin on the table. She gave him a brush.

Michael looked for orange paint. The orange jar was empty. "Oh no," said Michael. "No orange."

He found a jar of red paint. He found a jar of yellow paint. He put red on the pumpkin. Then he put yellow on top of the red. He moved his brush round and round.

The pumpkin turned orange! Michael opened his eyes wide. "Look, Grandma!" he said. Grandma smiled. "What a big orange pumpkin," she said.

Michael dipped his brush again. Red, then yellow, round and round. He painted a slimy green worm on his pumpkin too. Then he held it up to the window, so the sun could see.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Tomorrow is the day after today.
story:
Madelyn wanted to go to Lily's house. She wanted to go now. "Can we go now, Mama?" she asked. "Not now," said Mama. "We go tomorrow. First you sleep, then it is tomorrow." Madelyn frowned. Tomorrow felt far away.

Mama had an idea. She gave Madelyn a letter to draw on. "Draw a picture for Lily," she said. Madelyn drew a red cat and a big sun. She dropped her crayon under the table. She picked it up and kept drawing. The picture was very good.

Then Madelyn waited. She watched the sun go down out the window. She ate her dinner. She had a bath. She put on her soft pajamas. "Is it tomorrow now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "Sleep first, then tomorrow."

Madelyn got in bed. She put the letter by her shoes so she would not forget it. The letter was not stuck under anything. It sat right on top. Madelyn closed her eyes. She slept all night. In the morning the sun was up. "Is it tomorrow?" she asked. Mama smiled. "It is tomorrow now." Madelyn grabbed her letter. "Lily's house today!" she said. Mama took her hand. "Yes, today we go."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice.
story:
Hailey wanted to play blocks with Grandpa. She ran to the big room. "Grandpa!" she shouted. The baby was asleep in the little bed. The baby woke up and began to cry. Hailey felt sad. The baby was sad too.

Mommy picked the baby up. She rocked her soft and slow. Grandpa held up one finger by his mouth. Hailey looked at the sleeping baby. She took a big breath. Then she made her voice very small. "Grandpa," she whispered. "Play blocks now?" The room stayed quiet. The baby closed her eyes again.

Grandpa smiled and sat down on the floor. Hailey gave him the red blocks. He gave her the blue ones. They took turns putting one block on top. The tower grew tall. Outside, a truck went down the street. Inside, it was still nice and quiet. "More blocks," Hailey whispered.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Heavy and light are opposites.
story:
Carter wants to build a big tower at daycare. He finds a heavy box under the toy shelf. He pulls it. He pulls again. The box does not move. "Too big for me," he says.

Miss Ana brings a small pillow. It has a soft feather inside. Carter lifts it up high. It is so light! He puts the pillow on top of the heavy box. Now the box is a big, round bottom. The pillow is a small, soft top.

The tower is dirty, so Miss Ana wipes it with a wet cloth. The cloth is cold on Carter's hand. He waits while it dries. He waits some more. Then he pushes his tower slowly across the rug. Slow, slow, slow. Ben runs fast past him. Carter laughs and keeps going slow. "My tower can ride on top," he says, and pats the soft pillow.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A plant's roots grow down into the soil.
story:
Blake went to the garden center with Dad. She picked a young tomato plant. It had green leaves and a little stick.

Blake wanted to plant it in her pot. She filled the pot with soft brown soil. Then she saw a weed growing in the pot. "Go away, weed," she said.

Blake pulled the weed. Up it came. "Look!" she said. Long stringy roots hung down. "It has little feet!" Dad laughed. "Those are roots," he said. "A plant's roots grow down into the soil."

Blake tapped her tomato plant out of its cup. She saw roots there too. She made a deep hole. She set the roots down into the dark soil. She patted the soil with her hands.

The sun came out. Blake watered the pot. One drop, two drops, a big number of drops. "Grow, tomato," she said. "Grow your feet down low."

Soon a red tomato grew. Dad picked it. Blake took a taste. "Yum," she said. "My feet helped you stand up!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: After you sleep tonight and wake up, today will be called yesterday.
story:
Matteo did not want to sleep. He stood at his window. Snow was falling. Snow fell on the trees. Snow fell on the fence. Matteo pressed his face to the cold glass.

Today had been a good day. Today he made a snowman. Today he drank warm cocoa. Matteo had one more thing he wanted. He wanted to sled tomorrow. But first he had to sleep.

"Where does today go?" Matteo asked Dad. Dad tucked the blanket up to Matteo's chin. Dad kissed his warm cheek. "Sleep now," Dad said softly. "Sledding comes later." Matteo closed his eyes. He slept and slept.

When Matteo woke up, the sun was bright. He ran to the window. "Is it tomorrow?" he called. "It is tomorrow," said Dad. "And the snowman day? Now we call that yesterday." Matteo jumped up and down. Yesterday he made a snowman. Today he would sled. "Get your boots," said Dad, and held the door open wide.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: Rinsing under the water washes the soap off your hands.
story:
Harper went to the pharmacy with Dad. A sneaky germ had made her tummy sick. The pharmacist gave Dad some medicine. Then the pharmacist said, "Wash your hands, little one. Count to twenty with soap."

At home, Harper got the soap. She rubbed and rubbed. One, two, three, four. She counted all the way to twenty.

Then she looked at her hands. "Why are they still slippery?" she asked.

Dad smiled. "Try the water."

Harper held her hands under the water. The water washed the soap away. Her hands were not slippery anymore. They felt clean and smooth.

"Now can I eat my crackers?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Your hands are ready."

Harper pointed at the sink. "The soap went down the hole!"

A boy walked by with his mom. "Bye, slippery soap!" Harper called. Then she took a big, quick bite of her cracker.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Freshly fallen snow is white.
story:
Gabriel was at Grandma's house. Snow fell all morning. Gabriel wanted to draw the snow.

He took white paper and a red crayon. He drew his red sled. He drew his yellow hat. He drew green trees. But the snow would not show up. The white crayon looked like nothing on the white paper.

"Try blue paper," said Grandma. Gabriel found blue paper. He drew with the white crayon. The snow showed up! It looked soft and fresh, just like the snow outside. He added a red scarf and a yellow sun.

Grandma hung the picture by the window. Outside, a small bird landed on the snow. It left tiny marks, like little footprints. Gabriel laughed. "Now the snow has pictures too," he said.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Wet paint can smudge if you touch it.
story:
Eliana went to the art gallery with her mama. Big paintings hung on the walls. One painting was all red. One was all blue. One was all yellow. "Red, blue, yellow," Eliana said softly, like a song.

In the corner was a table with paint pots. Eliana dipped her brush in blue. Then she dipped it in yellow. She made a green line on her paper. Her eyes went wide. "Mama, look! Blue and yellow made green!" Then she made purple with red and blue.

Next to the table hung a little painting of a monkey. The monkey looked thirsty, holding a red cup. Eliana touched the monkey's cup. Her finger came back with red on it. A small fingerprint sat on the painting now. A gallery lady came over. "That paint is still wet," she said. "This one is dry. You can touch the frame."

Eliana sat down to paint a new monkey. This time she kept her fingers on her own paper. She waited while her green paint dried. Then she pointed at it. "Dry!" she said. "All done, green."

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: When you count, you say one number word for each object and count each object only once.
story:
Ethan stood at the snack table at school. He wanted to count the apples. His teacher put them in a line. Ethan pointed and counted, "One, two, three, four, five." But then his finger jumped back. "Six," he said, pointing at the same apple again. The girl next to him shook her head. "There are five apples," she said. Ethan frowned and looked at the line.

He tried again. This time he watched his finger. He touched each apple one time. "One, two, three, four, five." He did not touch any apple twice. Five! He counted them again just to be sure. One tap for each apple, and one number for each tap. He smiled big.

Then the teacher held up two bowls. One had crackers, one had grapes. "Which has more?" she asked. Ethan counted the crackers. He counted the grapes. "The grapes have more!" he said. He tapped his finger on the bowl and laughed.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: On a long drive, the family can stop at a rest stop so people can use the bathroom and stretch.
story:
Hannah sat on the big train with Mama and Dad. Rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap. Hannah liked to watch the rain slide down the glass.

Then her tummy made a squeeze. "I need to pee," she whispered. "Do we stop at a rest stop now?" In the car, they always did that. Daddy would park, and everyone would hop out and stretch.

Mama smiled a big smile. "Come with me," she said. She took Hannah's hand down the little aisle. Then she opened a small door. It was a tiny bathroom, right on the train!

"A bathroom on wheels!" said Hannah. She giggled so much she almost forgot to pee.

When she came out, Dad was holding something behind his back. "Look who came along," he said. It was Hannah's yellow sock monkey, waving from a seat by the window. "He watched the rain the whole time," said Dad.

Hannah gave the monkey a big squeeze and sat down to watch with him.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Diwali, many families light small clay oil lamps called diyas.
story:
Eleanor woke up excited. Today was Diwali! Grandma called her to the table. On it sat little clay lamps called diyas. There were so many! Eleanor touched one. It was cool and smooth.

"Can I help?" Eleanor asked. "Yes, you can help," said Grandma. Eleanor set out the diyas in a row. One, two, three, four, five. They all sat dark and empty.

"Who will make them glow?" Eleanor asked. Daddy struck the match. He tipped it into the first diya. A little flame popped up! Then he lit the next one, and the next. One flame made the whole row glow. The night outside was dark, but the room was bright. Eleanor clapped her messy, floury hands. "Happy Diwali!" she shouted. Grandma laughed and hugged her tight.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Peas grow inside pods on the plant.
story:
Sophie went to the garden with Grandma. She had little seeds in her hand. "Plant them here," said Grandma. Sophie pushed the seeds into the soft brown dirt. Then she patted the dirt down, pat, pat.

Sophie wanted her plants to grow. But day after day, nothing came up. "Where are my seeds?" she asked. "Wait," said Grandma. "Rain will help." The rain came down, drip, drip. The warm sun came out too. Soon little green leaves popped up. The plants grew tall. They curled up a stick like a pig's curly tail.

One day Sophie saw something green hanging on her plant. "What is that?" she asked. She picked it. It felt bumpy. Sophie turned it over in her hands. Then she popped it open. Inside was a row of little round peas! Sophie smiled big. "Look, Grandma!" she said. Grandma laughed and ate one. "Sweet peas from Sophie's garden."
